text: You already know a field-level ACL is checked in addition to the table-level ACL for the same operation, never instead of it. This lesson is about the real design patterns for using that field-level layer well, on genuinely sensitive fields.

The standard pattern is deny by default, allow by exception. Rather than listing every role that shouldn't see a salary figure, you list only the narrow set that should. This script checks membership in a compensation group or a specific admin role -- a deliberately short exception list.

Trace it for a user who holds only hr_admin -- a broad, powerful-sounding role elsewhere in the platform. isMemberOf comes back false, hasRole for the compensation-admin role comes back false, so the script sets answer equals false and salary_band stays hidden. Field-level security only cares about the specific exception list this one field was scoped to, not what else the user can do.

A field-level ACL is a binary gate -- visible or not, pass or fail. Data Anonymization, covered in depth in Chapter 4, is the natural second layer on the same field: it can mask a value for users who technically pass the ACL but still shouldn't see the full number. The ACL answers whether a user can see the field at all; anonymization answers how much of it they actually see. Together, that's defense in depth -- two independent layers on one sensitive field.

This is a genuine balancing act. Over-restrict the field, and you break real workflows -- someone who legitimately needs the data can't do their job, and escalates constantly or works around it. Under-restrict it, and the field is exposed to people with no legitimate need, which is exactly the risk field-level ACLs exist to prevent. A well-designed instance works out the real, specific minimum access each role genuinely needs, field by field.
Deny by default, layer in anonymization, and aim for the genuine minimum each role needs. Next up: the Advanced ACL Lab, where you'll write and trace a field-level ACL like this one end to end.
